key_terms.meaning: A shallow parameterised circuit U(θ) whose rotation angles θ the classical optimiser tunes; depth is kept small because near-term hardware has noisy gates.
A hybrid loop that minimises the measured energy ⟨ψ(θ)|H|ψ(θ)⟩ of a problem Hamiltonian H; for molecules the minimum is the ground-state energy.
A variational loop whose circuit alternates a cost layer e^(−iγC) and a mixer layer e^(−iβB), repeated p times on |+⟩ⁿ, to minimise a combinatorial cost C.
The shot-averaged energy: run the circuit many times, read each measured bit-string's energy, and average weighted by counts.
Ordinary software (COBYLA, SPSA, Nelder–Mead) that takes the measured energy and returns the next angle vector θ; it never touches the quantum state.
An operator written as a sum of Pauli strings, for example H = Σ hᵢ Zᵢ + Σ Jᵢⱼ ZᵢZⱼ, whose eigenvalues are the cost values of candidate bit-strings.
K(x, x′) = |⟨φ(x′)|φ(x)⟩|², a similarity between two data points obtained by applying feature map U(x), then U(x′)†, and measuring the all-zero outcome.
A circuit U(x) that loads a classical vector x into a quantum state |φ(x)⟩ using rotation angles or amplitudes; the choice of map fixes the kernel.
A support vector is a training point lying on the class boundary; the margin is the gap the classifier maximises between the two classes. Both are found classically once kernel values are known.
A circuit prepares a state and measures a few observables; a classical layer turns those numbers into a loss and updates the circuit angles.
Demonstrations with a handful of qubits: images of a few pixels, sentences of a few tokens. Realistic data does not fit.
On every published language or vision task, quantum models match or trail classical deep learning; no speed or accuracy gain is established.
Quadratic Unconstrained Binary Optimization: minimise xᵀQx with xᵢ ∈ {0,1}. Any QUBO maps to an Ising Hamiltonian by substituting xᵢ = (1 − Zᵢ)/2.
A Grover-based routine that estimates a probability amplitude to accuracy ε using about 1/ε queries instead of 1/ε², the basis of quadratic speedups in Monte Carlo pricing.
The eigenvalue of an electronic Hamiltonian, mapped to qubits by a fermion-to-qubit transform; VQE estimates it to compare catalysts or battery electrolytes.
Choosing which generators to switch on in each time block to meet demand at least cost; a binary decision problem that fits a QUBO.
Computing the expected discounted payoff of a derivative; expressed as a Monte Carlo average, it is a candidate for amplitude estimation.
Classical algorithms (lattice, code, hash based) designed to resist both classical and quantum attack; standardised because Shor's algorithm breaks RSA and elliptic-curve keys.
Grover search gives a quadratic speedup, so a 256-bit symmetric key behaves like a 128-bit key against a quantum attacker; doubling the key restores the margin.
The same machine that designs a drug or a catalyst can help design a weapon or break a cipher; the technology cannot be split into safe and unsafe halves.

takeaways: VQE and QAOA are the same idea applied to two different cost operators: a shallow circuit guesses an answer, hardware measures its cost, a classical optimiser improves the guess.
The quantum part of a variational algorithm only prepares a state and measures; every optimisation step and every bookkeeping task stays classical.
A quantum kernel is a similarity measure computed by a circuit, so a support vector machine can use it while its margins and support vectors remain classical numbers.
Quantum language and vision models are laboratory toys today, and no published result shows them beating classical deep networks on a real task.
Industry treats the quantum computer as one solver inside an existing classical pipeline: map the problem, run the solver, then verify and refine classically.
Chemistry, materials, finance and logistics differ mostly in how the problem is mapped to a Hamiltonian or a QUBO, not in the quantum subroutine used.
Every experimental claim should carry its status — simulation only, small hardware run, or production — because most published applications are early stage.
A future fault-tolerant machine breaks RSA and elliptic-curve cryptography, so migrating to post-quantum schemes is an engineering deadline, not a research option.
Access, bias, energy cost and privacy are design questions for quantum machine learning, not afterthoughts.
bank_note: Long answers are marked on the closed loop: how the problem becomes a Hamiltonian or QUBO, what the circuit measures, how the classical optimiser closes the loop, and an honest statement of present-day status.

bank.q: Describe the VQE loop step by step for finding the ground-state energy of a small molecule. State clearly which parts run on the quantum processor and which on the classical computer.
outline: Fermionic Hamiltonian from the molecular problem, mapped to qubits as a sum of Pauli strings.
Choose a shallow ansatz that respects the problem's symmetries and particle number.
Prepare |ψ(θ)⟩ on hardware and measure each Pauli string by rotating into its basis.
Sum the measured expectations into ⟨H⟩(θ) with the known coefficients.
Pass ⟨H⟩ to a classical optimiser, get new θ, repeat until the energy stops falling.
The variational principle guarantees ⟨H⟩ ≥ E₀, so the estimate is an upper bound.

bank.q: Explain QAOA and contrast it with VQE. Why does QAOA use a mixer layer, and what does the depth p control?
outline: Start from |+⟩ⁿ; apply cost layer e^(−iγC) and mixer layer e^(−iβB) alternately p times.
The cost layer imprints phases proportional to the cost of each bit-string.
The mixer layer moves amplitude between bit-strings so the circuit can explore.
Parameters γ₁…γ_p, β₁…β_p are tuned classically to minimise ⟨C⟩.
Difference from VQE: the ansatz is fixed by the problem (mixer plus phase separator), not chosen freely.
Larger p gives a richer circuit and better approximation at the price of depth and noise.

bank.q: What is a quantum kernel? Show how it is estimated on a quantum computer from two data points x and x′, and explain why the rest of the SVM stays classical.
outline: Define |φ(x)⟩ = U(x)|0…0⟩ with a feature-map circuit.
Circuit: apply U(x), then U(x′)†, measure; probability of the all-zero outcome is the kernel value.
Repeat over shots to estimate the probability.
The kernel matrix feeds a classical convex optimiser for αᵢ.
Support vectors, margins and the decision function are classical arithmetic.

bank.q: Define a QUBO and an Ising Hamiltonian. Show the substitution that converts one into the other, and give one reason a problem is put in this form.
outline: QUBO: minimise xᵀQx with xᵢ ∈ {0,1}.
Ising: H = Σ hᵢ Zᵢ + Σ Jᵢⱼ ZᵢZⱼ with eigenvalues ±1.
Substitute xᵢ = (1 − Zᵢ)/2 and collect terms.
Constraint penalties can be added as large diagonal or quadratic terms.
Reason: hardware and variational algorithms are built to minimise expectation values of such operators.

bank.q: Write a QAOA-style cost Hamiltonian for max-cut on a triangle (three vertices, all edges present) and interpret the two degenerate ground states.
outline: Label qubits 1, 2, 3; a bit says which side of the cut a vertex falls on.
Cost C = sum over edges of (1 − ZᵢZⱼ)/2, maximised for a good cut.
Sign flip converts maximisation to minimisation for a variational loop.
Ground states are the two colourings 001-type arrangements where one vertex is alone.
Maximum cut value is 2 of 3 edges; the other cuts give 2 as well on a triangle — check the arithmetic honestly.

bank.q: Formulate a three-city symmetric travelling salesman problem as a QUBO suitable for QAOA: state the binary variables, the objective terms and the penalty terms.
outline: Variable x_{i,t} = 1 if city i is visited at position t; n² binary variables.
Objective: sum of edge costs times products of consecutive-position variables.
Penalty one: each city visited exactly once — (Σ_t x_{i,t} − 1)².
Penalty two: each position holds exactly one city.
Total H = objective + λ(penalties), with λ large enough to forbid invalid tours.
Note the qubit count grows as n² and the landscape is hard for shallow circuits.

bank.q: A bank wants to price a European option by quantum amplitude estimation. Outline the pipeline from the classical Monte Carlo formula to the estimated price, and say what the speedup is.
outline: Price = discounted expectation of the payoff; classically a Monte Carlo average with error ~ 1/√M.
Load the return distribution into qubit amplitudes with a state-preparation circuit.
Encode the payoff into a rotation so its amplitude equals the quantity to be averaged.
Amplitude estimation recovers that amplitude to accuracy ε with about 1/ε iterations.
Quadratic improvement in the error-versus-queries scaling, not an exponential one.
Caveat: distribution loading and payoff arithmetic dominate the cost and are being researched.

bank.q: Sketch a four-qubit-circuit experiment to classify two classes of two-pixel images using a quantum kernel, and list every classical step around it.
outline: Angle-encode each image's two pixel values into rotation angles of a feature-map circuit.
Compute the kernel matrix by pairwise overlap circuits, many shots each.
Feed the matrix to a classical SVM solver with a regularisation constant.
Test on held-out images; report accuracy honestly against a classical baseline.
Classical steps: encoding choice, kernel matrix assembly, training, thresholding, error bars.
State the limit: two pixels is a toy; scaling encoding is unsolved.

bank.q: Explain why quantum kernel methods can stall as the number of qubits grows, and discuss the mitigation strategies and their costs.
outline: Concentration: for many feature maps the overlap of two random states tends to a fixed value, so kernel values cluster and the matrix looks uniform.
A uniform kernel carries little class information; the classifier degenerates to guessing.
Measuring overlaps needs exponentially many shots for high precision as the value concentrates.
Mitigations: problem-inspired feature maps, fewer qubits, classical pre-reduction of the data, bandwidth tuning.
Each mitigation trades away either expressivity or the claimed quantum benefit.
Conclusion: kernel advantage is problem specific and must be demonstrated, not assumed.

bank.q: Assess the claim that quantum computers will soon replace classical deep learning for language and vision. Use the evidence available from published toy experiments.
outline: Published quantum language and vision models use a few qubits and a few pixels or tokens.
Data loading costs grow quickly; encoding a real image is itself hard.
No experiment reports accuracy or wall-clock gain over standard classical networks.
Classical hardware also improves each year, raising the bar.
Honest position: quantum is a candidate co-processor for specific subroutines, not a replacement.
Correct framing of the near-term goal: find a structured problem with provable separation.

bank.q: Compare VQE, QAOA and quantum kernel methods on the same axes: what they optimise, what circuit they need, what classical algorithm sits beside them, and what they are used for.
outline: VQE: minimises ⟨H⟩, needs a chemistry-inspired ansatz, classical optimiser, used for molecular energies.
QAOA: minimises a cost function, needs alternating cost and mixer layers, classical optimiser, used for combinatorial problems.
Kernel method: needs no optimisation on hardware, estimates overlaps, classical SVM or logistic regression, used for classification.
All three need many shots per parameter setting and share noise and trainability problems.
Kernel methods avoid the parameter landscape but need a good feature map.
Selection depends on whether the problem is an eigenvalue problem, a discrete optimisation or a classification.

bank.q: Discuss the societal and security impact of a large fault-tolerant quantum computer: cryptography migration, access and equity, bias in quantum models, energy cost and dual use.
outline: Shor's algorithm breaks RSA and elliptic-curve key exchange; Grover halves symmetric key strength, so double key lengths.
Migration to post-quantum schemes is an engineering programme with inventory, testing and rollout phases.
Harvest-now-decrypt-later makes long-lived secrets urgent today.
Access: hardware is scarce and costly, so benefits may concentrate.
Bias: quantum models trained on biased data reproduce the bias, and kernel choices add opacity.
Energy: dilution refrigerators and control electronics draw continuous power, so the cost per answer matters.
Dual use: the same simulation capability serves medicine and weapons research; governance must be designed in.

bank.q: A distribution company wants to try quantum optimisation for vehicle routing. Design an end-to-end hybrid pipeline and state where the quantum part helps, where it cannot, and what you would report to management.
outline: Classical front end: clean the data, cluster customers, fix a subset of routes.
Map the reduced problem to a QUBO: binary variables for stops per route, penalties for capacity and time windows.
Convert to an Ising Hamiltonian by xᵢ = (1 − Zᵢ)/2.
Run QAOA or a variational solver on the small instance; sample bit-strings.
Classical back end: repair infeasible samples, verify with a classical solver, compare to a strong heuristic baseline.
Report status honestly: toy-to-small instances only, no production advantage shown.
Keep the classical solver in charge; the quantum machine is an optional sampler.

bank.q: Describe amplitude estimation, relate it to Grover's diffusion operator and to phase estimation, and evaluate which financial and counting tasks can use it.
outline: Grover iteration: mark the good subspace with a phase, then diffuse about the mean amplitude.
After k iterations the amplitude of the good subspace is sin((2k+1)θ), where sin²θ is the probability being estimated.
Quantum phase estimation on the Grover operator reads θ, hence the amplitude, to accuracy ε with O(1/ε) operator calls.
Classical Monte Carlo needs O(1/ε²) samples for the same error — the quadratic gain.
Uses: option pricing, risk aggregation, counting, integration.
Limits: state preparation of the distribution, arithmetic depth and the missing fault-tolerant hardware.

glossary.def: For any normalised trial state, the measured energy is never below the true ground-state energy, so a variational estimate is a safe upper bound.
A region where the gradient of the measured cost with respect to the circuit angles vanishes exponentially in qubit count, stalling training.
A product such as X⊗Z⊗I on named qubits; Hamiltonians on quantum hardware are written as weighted sums of Pauli strings.
Statistical error from running a circuit a finite number of times; it falls as 1/√N for N shots.
The squared overlap |⟨ψ|φ⟩|² between two quantum states, the quantity that a quantum kernel estimates.
Replacing inner products with a similarity function K(x, x′) so a linear classifier works in a richer feature space.
Storing a classical number as a rotation angle, for example R_y(θ)|0⟩, so n features cost n qubits.
Storing a vector in the 2ⁿ amplitudes of an n-qubit state; compact but the preparation circuit may be long.
Applying the same feature map several times with trainable layers between, shown to increase the expressivity of small circuits.
An energy function of spin variables Zᵢ = ±1 with linear and pairwise couplings, the natural input format of a quantum optimiser.
Splitting a graph's vertices into two groups so that as many edges as possible cross between them.
Noisy intermediate-scale quantum: machines with tens to a few hundred noisy qubits, without error correction.
Operation with logical error rates low enough for arbitrarily long algorithms by using many physical qubits per logical qubit.
Predicting how a drug molecule binds to a protein target; a candidate for quantum optimisation, still at toy scale.
Choosing asset weights to balance return against risk; the binary-cardinality version maps to a QUBO.
Assigning a fleet to deliver to many stops at least cost; the combinatorial form maps to a QUBO.
Recording encrypted traffic today in order to decrypt it once a large quantum computer exists.
Search by repeated marking and diffusion that finds one item among N in about √N steps.
A routine using the inverse quantum Fourier transform to read the eigenvalue phase of a unitary; the engine behind Shor's algorithm and amplitude estimation.
A quantum algorithm for factoring integers in polynomial time, which breaks RSA and elliptic-curve cryptography.
Systematic unfairness in a model's outputs, inherited from the training data or from modelling choices; quantum models do not remove it.
The electrical power needed to run a dilution refrigerator and its control electronics, a real operating cost of any quantum data centre.
The total facility power divided by problem solves per unit time; the fair comparison metric against classical machines.
